entry.title: On the Convergence of Iterated Round Robin
entry.summary: Round Robin (RR) is a simple and widely used picking sequence mechanism for allocating indivisible goods, known to guarantee envy-freeness up to one item (EF1) when preferences are additive. Despite being manipulable (meaning that agents may have an incentive to strategically misreport their preferences), it is known to always admit at least one pure Nash equilibrium. In this paper, we study an iterated variant of RR, in which agents observe the outcome of the mechanism at each iteration and may revise their reported preferences through a best-response dynamics. We first consider a full-information setting, where agents observe both the outcome and the reported preferences of all the agents. In this setting, we show that cycles can occur even under strong restrictions on the manipulations carried out by the agents. We nonetheless identify a natural restriction (item-preserving swaps), under which convergence to a pure Nash equilibrium is guaranteed to exist for any number of agents and items. We also show that restricting to adjacent swaps guarantees convergence for two agents and a limited number of items, leaving the question open for unbounded number of items. We then turn to a partial-information setting, in which agents only observe the resulting allocation and must then infer the preference profiles of the others assuming consistency with the RR sequence. We study three behaviours guiding the agents when deciding how to manipulate under uncertainty on the other agents' preferences. We show that two of the studied behaviours, despite being quite natural, may cycle while a more cautious rule guarantees iterated RR to be strategyproof.

entry.title: Cooperation Without Adaptation: LLM Agents in a Collective-Risk Dilemma
entry.summary: Language-model agents are increasingly deployed to act on behalf of people in settings where individual decisions shape shared outcomes. We examine whether five production models adapt their contributions to changing risks and partner behaviour, or instead follow a relatively fixed strategy. In a collective-risk dilemma game (CRG), six players contribute to a shared pool over ten rounds; if the pool falls short of its target, a catastrophe may destroy their remaining resources. Four models contributed approximately an equal share at every positive risk level, and four of the five also contributed when risk was zero, even though contributing could not improve their payoff. Explicitly stating that only the agent's own payoff mattered reduced zero-risk contributions for most models, while a more neutral prompt did not. Several models correctly identified which action offered the higher expected payoff at different risk levels, yet their contributions changed little. Against fixed partners, no model consistently chose the payoff-maximising response, and in mixed-model groups, a single agent's shortfall in the final round could cause an otherwise successful group to fail. Payoff-based selection also depended on population composition: in a single six-agent group, it favoured the model that contributed least and reduced group success, whereas in larger, randomly mixed populations, it favoured an exact fair-share model at moderate and high risk. These findings show that cooperative self-play alone is not evidence of strategic adaptability. Consistent with a machine-behaviour approach, evaluations of agents in multi-agent systems should test how they respond to incentives, partner actions, and population composition.

entry.title: The Source of Data Value: Consumer Disclosure, Access Design, and Platform Monetization
entry.summary: Digital marketplaces increasingly earn revenue from transaction commissions and seller-facing data services. Sellers may purchase data to increase revenue or avoid competing with an informed rival. We examine how consumer disclosure rights shape these motives and the platform's incentive to provide data. We develop a game-theoretic model of a commissioned platform, two differentiated sellers, and privacy-sensitive consumers. Data generates value through bilateral sales-revenue gains and competition threats arising from asymmetric access. Under mandatory collection, the platform can monetize defensive adoption, even when bilateral personalization reduces seller revenue. Under voluntary disclosure, anonymous purchasing and strictly positive privacy costs make unilateral disclosure unattractive in the baseline. Exclusive access thus yields no usable information, restores sellers' no-data rejection payoffs, and eliminates defensive fees. Profitable provision therefore requires nonnegative bilateral revenue gains. Under full fee extraction, sellers retain their no-data net profits. This revenue alignment does not guarantee welfare gains: additional transactions may benefit consumers, whereas segmentation in an already covered market can raise anonymous prices and reduce welfare. Capping anonymous offers at their no-data benchmark protects individual consumers and limits positive-mass provision to the transaction-creation region. Extensions consider access choice, heterogeneous privacy costs, imperfect identification, and limited contractual credibility. Platforms should evaluate data services based on both bilateral-use and seller-rejection outcomes, and sellers should distinguish revenue-enhancing from defensive investments. Regulators should distinguish equal-access rules from effective consumer control and monitor pricing in anonymous channels.

entry.title: Optimally Curating an Event
entry.summary: We study the optimal design of a self-financing event, a problem that requires balancing the recruitment of costly, positive-value participants with revenue-generating agents who may impose negative values on the event. We introduce a novel two-sided mechanism design framework with plus agents equipped with private costs and positive impact, and minus agents with private values and negative impact upon inclusion in the event, to maximize the overall quality of the event under a budget-balanced (BB) constraint so that the designer does not run a deficit. We conduct a comprehensive study on the theory of optimal event curation on various utility functions. For additive utility, we fully characterize the optimal incentive-compatible Bayesian mechanism under both the ex-ante and ex-post BB constraints. For submodular utility, we propose an ex-ante BB mechanism that achieves a constant-factor approximation to the optimal Bayesian mechanism.

entry.title: Anytime Contracts for AI Services
entry.summary: AI services are prone to moral hazard, as model providers can silently route requests to cheaper, lower-quality models, and the inherent stochasticity of model outputs makes this degradation hard to detect. Contract theory addresses moral hazard by designing payment rules that reward high-quality outputs and prevent strategic overcharging. However, existing frameworks assume interactions of fixed duration, whereas AI services are typically consumed through subscriptions and pay-as-you-go APIs that users can terminate at any time based on observed performance. We show that this flexibility can break standard contracts, opening them up to abuse by either the providers or users. To address this, we extend contract theory to account for unknown exit rules. We formalize the problem as a Principal-Agent game, and show that budget-optimal contracts in this setting are proportional to anytime-valid hypothesis tests based on likelihood-ratio e-values. We give an efficient algorithm for computing anytime contracts and show how betting e-processes can be used to approximate them when the models are unknown. Finally, we evaluate our findings on synthetic data and data from deployed LLMs.

entry.title: Dynamic Auction Mechanisms in a Closed-Credit Economy: Sequential Slot Reallocation in Air Traffic Management
entry.summary: Indivisible resources allocated in advance may need to be reallocated when capacity reductions make existing assignments infeasible, yet monetary compensation is often impractical or undesirable. We develop a sequential resource reallocation scheme using reusable artificial credits, where agents hold pre-existing resource rights and have heterogeneous marginal valuations over time blocks. Capacity reductions produce fractional endowments, which our closed-credit scheme resolves into indivisible final allocations. We model agents' intertemporal preferences through a predicted-value-to-go function and characterize conditions ensuring that their optimal demand is non-increasing in price. We propose an ascending-auction mechanism that partitions agents into subgroups and uses the minimum subgroup market-clearing price as a common transaction price. We show that the mechanism preserves non-myopic individual rationality and weak nontrader neutrality. Moreover, we establish Pareto efficiency under optimal-demand clearing in the unified market and bound the expected gain from misreporting by the probability that an agent changes the common price. Simulations of airport slot reallocation demonstrate reductions in total modeled delay and cancellation costs relative to a ground-delay baseline.

entry.title: StratFL: Countering Covert Model Poisoning Attacks with Strategic Federated Learning
entry.summary: Advanced persistent threats (APTs) are a major concern in federated learning (FL) deployments in critical sectors such as healthcare, and finance. Traditional defense mechanisms fail to contain APTs due to their intermittent attacking behavior. This paper addresses a specific type of APT called covert model poisoning (CMP) where the attacker intermittently injects poisoned model updates in a covert manner. The interaction between the FL server and a CMP attacker is modeled as an imperfect repeated game where both players cannot observe each other's actions. A novel adversarial search algorithm called StratFL is designed alongside novel belief update algorithms at both the server and adversary. Experiments are designed using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets to evaluate and compare StratFL's performance against state-of-the-art methods. Empirical convergence of belief update algorithms is demonstrated across various security vignettes. At the same time, StratFL is found to exhibit an improved accuracy of 10% compared to state-of-the-art methods.

entry.title: Auditable and Deployable Multi-Agent Motion Planning via Posetal Games from Legal Guidelines
entry.summary: When robots are deployed in the real-world, they must interact with other agents and accomplish their own goals while adhering to legal constraints. These potentially conflicting objectives are often only partially prioritized, making scalarized objectives or fully specified hierarchies unsuitable. We present a framework for multi-agent motion planning under legal requirements based on games with partially ordered preferences (posetal games). Scenario-independent legal guidelines order abstract legal concerns, from which we automatically derive agent preferences and a legal game for any concrete scenario. Agents may refine their legal preferences with private objectives, and regulators may refine the guideline as laws evolve. We prove that such customizations can only remove equilibria and thus preserve legality. To coordinate agents without explicitly communicating private preferences, we introduce belief play, which provably recovers the true equilibria from conservative local games, and a distributed iterative best-response protocol requiring less information. We apply the framework to maritime navigation, systematically lifting pairwise traffic rules to multi-vessel encounters. On seven encounters with up to four vessels, every rule violation of the committed equilibria is certified as forced by the legal hierarchy or unsatisfiable, and defectors are identified from public information in all tested cases. These results indicate that guideline-based posetal games offer an auditable route from partially specified laws to multi-agent motion planning.

entry.title: Decentralized LLM Workflows via Sequential Auctions
entry.summary: We present a scalable framework for solving multi-step tasks through a decentralized market of self-interested agents. Prior theoretical work demonstrated that agents organized through sequential auctions can converge to a globally optimal policy in a Markov decision process (MDP), but relied on the restrictive assumption of the existence of perfect clones as a model of perfect competition. In reality, exact clones drive agent profit to zero, violating the natural risk-reward incentives of participants. Conversely, we empirically demonstrate that the opposite extreme, absence of competition, also leads to market failure and value extraction collapse. Between these two extremes, we investigate how heterogeneous agents can survive in markets that span the critical middle ground of imperfect competition. To be profitable, agents learn to strategically shade bids to secure positive individual profit margins, while still ensuring that the marketplace functions effectively enough so that collaborative tasks posed by market consumers can still be solved. We formulate and evaluate four bidding algorithms (Mirror Descent, Thompson Sampling, Bayes-Optimal, and PPO) across three auction protocols (1st-Price, 2nd-Price, and Credit-Conserving Vickrey). Across a diverse set of domains, we demonstrate that imperfect competition successfully sustains necessary agent profit margins while maintaining high task success rates at low costs.

entry.title: Smoothed analysis of policy iteration and value iteration for deterministic discounted and mean-payoff games played on any graph
entry.summary: Our understanding of turn-based stochastic games is reminiscent of our understanding of linear programming in the 1970s. Instead of the simplex method, we have two families of algorithms - policy iteration and value iteration - which work well in practice but are known to run in exponential time on some input instances, and we still lack an algorithm that runs in polynomial time on all instances. A recent result by Loff and Skomra showed that, for deterministic discounted and mean-payoff games played on an ergodic graph, a variant of policy iteration runs in smoothed polynomial time. This offered an explanation of why policy iteration performs well in practice, analogous to Spielman and Teng's explanation for the simplex method. In this paper, we drop the ergodicity assumption: we show that their policy iteration algorithms run in smoothed polynomial time for any game graph. We do this by defining a condition number that naturally generalizes theirs, showing that sufficiently-perturbed games are well-conditioned with high probability, and showing that their algorithms are efficient on well-conditioned instances. Although the outline is similar, our proof requires a substantially new approach, based on log-Lipschitz distributions which recently appeared in work on the smoothed analysis of the simplex method. For our second contribution, we propose three new value iteration algorithms for solving deterministic mean-payoff games (also on any graph). All three are based on iterative methods for finding fixed points of non-expansive operators, which we show can be applied to the Shapley operator. The first two are simple applications of Krasnoselskii-Mann iteration and Halpern iteration. The third is quadratically faster but more complicated: it runs Zwick-Paterson and Halpern iterations in parallel. We prove that all three algorithms are correct and run in smoothed polynomial time.

entry.title: Why Alternation Speeds Up Counterfactual Regret Minimization?
entry.summary: Solving imperfect-information games at scale rests on counterfactual regret minimization with the regret matching$^{+}$ (RM$^{+}$) update, and a seemingly minor implementation choice accounts for much of its practical speed: alternating the two players' updates, so that the second player responds to the strategy the first player just produced. A widely repeated intuition explains why: seeing the opponent's fresh strategy should act like optimism. We treat this intuition as a testable hypothesis about deterministic two-player zero-sum self-play dynamics and find that its canonical additive form fails an information-matched test. On an analytic witness family we compare alternating RM$^{+}$ against a one-sided predictive RM$^{+}$ that receives the same information channel each round and differs only in where the fresh signal enters, a persistent regret state versus a transient prediction term. Our main result is a dichotomy theorem that reduces trajectory separation to the recurrence of exact-vertex play by the predictive dynamics: under an interior-band assumption on the alternating iterate, either vertex times recur and the profile distance is at least, infinitely often, an explicit constant that our measurements nearly attain, or they terminate. Across the tested self-play regimes, any correct explanation of the alternation speedup must reproduce a staleness cost present at the smallest tested stale fraction, an advantage that persists across seven orders of payoff conditioning, regime crossings of the optimism family, and a measured per-perturbation cost of weakening the injection path that is far steeper for staleness than for partial persistence.

entry.title: Learning Rewards in Strategic Games
entry.summary: Understanding the objectives that drive agents' behavior is crucial in strategic environments, where multiple agents interact and adapt to one another. This challenge arises in domains such as cybersecurity, autonomous driving, and online markets, where agents' underlying incentives are typically unknown and must be inferred from their observed behavior. Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a natural framework for this problem, but extending IRL to strategic multi-agent settings introduces a fundamental challenge: a reward that explains observed behavior does not necessarily induce optimal strategies when used for decision-making. In this work, we study this problem through the lens of \emph{strategic identifiability}, and show that learning from a fixed policy pair can be insufficient to strategically identify rewards, independent of the number of expert samples $K$. Motivated by this, we introduce an active IRL algorithm for two-player repeated Stackelberg games, in which the leader adaptively selects policies to elicit informative responses about the follower's reward. Combining maximum-likelihood estimation with experimental design, we derive finite-sample guarantees on the Stackelberg sub-optimality induced by the learned reward, matching up to polylogarithmic factors a new minimax learning rate of $K^{-1/2}$. Finally, we evaluate our approach in a realistic anti-poaching setting, demonstrating the benefits of active exploration for reward recovery and downstream strategic performance.

entry.title: How language model agents reshape price competition
entry.summary: Repeated Bertrand competition is a stringent benchmark for algorithmic pricing: in homogeneous-goods markets, standard learning procedures typically select the stage-game Nash outcome with prices near marginal cost. We show that LLM pricing agents can escape this benchmark, depending on deployment decisions. LLMs outperform standard online learners through faster adaptation, but this advantage largely disappears against full-information learners. An extracted surrogate algorithm illustrates how LLMs in specific deployments profit from regularly undercutting slower learners. Agents that post one price every period from raw market histories that include rival prices can sustain supracompetitive regimes in self-play. Agents that periodically emit probability distributions from summarized histories of their own profits instead move toward the competitive region in self-play. Markets mixing these interfaces can generate dynamic regimes in which LLMs establish a high-price anchor and regularly undercut it to capture demand. These regimes can keep both competitors' prices above marginal cost. Deployment choices shape these outcomes, shifting the focus from stationary equilibria to dynamic pricing regimes.

entry.title: Market Incentives for AI Safety Investment
entry.summary: Despite their practical significance, modern AI systems pose significant societal risks, including toxicity, malicious use, and misinformation. Their mitigation depends not only on technical feasibility but also on the incentives of firms that develop and deploy these systems. We show how profit maximization shapes safety investment in an AI supply chain with an upstream LLM provider and several competing downstream firms. In our game-theoretic model, we derive the market-driven level of safety investment and compare it with the levels that maximize market welfare and industry profit. We find that downstream competition generally induces downstream firms to invest more in safety than the industry-profit-optimal level. By contrast, the upstream provider may underinvest relative to these benchmarks because it is not fully compensated for the surplus from safety investments. Finally, we analyze how different regulatory interventions affect the participants' incentives and profits, and the resulting levels of model safety.

entry.title: Approximating the Value of Time-Bounded Weighted Timed Games
entry.summary: The Value Problem for weighted timed games, an extension of timed automata with weights and adversity, consists in determining, given a weighted timed game with a reachability objective and a rational threshold, whether or not the value of the game exceeds the threshold. This problem is known to be undecidable for weighted timed games, i.e., there is no algorithm that can compute the value exactly. A natural alternative is to approximate the value; however, the Approximation problem is also undecidable in general. In this paper, we prove that the Approximation problem is decidable in 4-ExpTime for weighted timed games whose executions are time-bounded.

entry.title: An autocomplete model for elections
entry.summary: We consider two linked problems for ranked choice elections: building a compact summary of a preference profile $P$, and generating synthetic profiles that resemble $P$ in key ways. We introduce a Markov model based on which candidate names follow which on observed ballots and record this in a succession matrix on candidates together with a start/stop symbol. This provides the basis for new ``autocomplete'' methods for generating synthetic profiles, with ballot length that can be tuned to a target. We compare succession-based generation to parallel use of summaries built from positional frequencies and head-to-head comparisons. To execute this comparison, we introduce new descriptive statistics of profiles that allow new tests of whether synthetic profiles are realistic. In experiments on Scottish ranked-choice profiles, succession-based generation captures held-out ballot structure well, performs especially strongly when completing partial ballots, and often preserves election outcomes, outperforming the alternatives on all counts. Finally, we study the dynamics of iterating the train-and-generate process.

entry.title: Price of Anarchy of First-Price Auctions in Agentic Markets
entry.summary: An agentic market is a decentralized serving-time market where AI agents bid to claim each user prompt. An agent's bid is based on its expected value for the prompt, which is the expectation of the reward for its response minus its inference costs. First-price auctions (FPAs), in which the highest bidder pays its bid and receives the prompt, are a natural way to allocate prompts in such a market, since they are simple and transparent to run, and do not require central knowledge of private capabilities and costs. However, FPAs are not truthful: participants may bid less than their true value in the hope of a larger profit, and the prompt may then be allocated to someone other than the bidder who values it the most. This welfare loss is quantified by the $\textit{price-of-anarchy}$ (PoA). In this paper, we argue that agentic markets are likely to possess features that reduce the price-of-anarchy. The first is a $\textit{competitive floor}$, which occurs when multiple bidders usually value the prompt above some baseline share of the optimal welfare (e.g., because the best models are often distilled into cheaper alternatives, which perform similarly). We show that competition among them then limits the welfare loss, which can be driven to zero as the floor rises. The second feature is $\textit{near-independence}$ of values after conditioning on the prompt, which occurs when most of the predictable variation in the expected value is determined by the difficulty of the prompt. As the value distribution approaches conditional independence, we can derive an efficiency guarantee that approaches a factor of $1 - 1/e^2$ of the optimal welfare. Thus, both features give rise to welfare lower bounds that are significantly better than the well-known general case of $1 - 1/e$. We validate these results empirically using auctions with strategic bidders simulated on the EmbedLLM prompt routing dataset.

entry.title: SafeAdapt-Poker: Counterfactual Risk Calibration for Budgeted Adaptation under Opponent Shift
entry.summary: Opponent histories can mislead after behavioral shifts. SafeAdapt-Poker formulates budgeted adaptation under opponent shift as a dual-counterfactual sequential-control problem using only information available before each decision. At each decision the controller asks two distinct questions: what local downside a deviation from the frozen anchor would induce under matched legal continuations, and what future adaptation value would be lost by consuming part of the remaining deviation budget now. The first question is answered by a monotone strategic-risk model over deviation intensity; the second by a paired budget-state continuation model that prices current budget consumption. The controller selects among support-preserving candidate deviations by trading immediate adaptation value against these two quantities, a pathwise cumulative-KL ledger bounds total anchor-relative deviation, and a finite family of frozen controllers is screened on complete paired calibration sessions before held-out interaction. A finite-candidate perturbation bound shows that the allocation objective degrades continuously with continuation-value estimation error. Evaluation covers exact-game exploitation and safety, four opponent shifts, local-risk calibration, delayed-opportunity allocation, direct opportunity-value estimation, value-error robustness, factorial mechanism attribution, budget sensitivity, abstract-HUNL cross-play, and player/time-held-out public-history behavior. On exact Leduc the full controller attains a matched weak-pool gain of +0.0718 with a worst-opponent delta of -0.0126, raises delayed-opportunity capture from 0.6318 under myopic allocation to 0.7841 under the same session budget, and reaches +42.7 mbb/hand in abstract-HUNL cross-play; the retained public-history screen reports 0.5820 action accuracy and 0.9277 log loss versus 0.5039 and 0.9778 for a public prior.

entry.title: What Does Disagreement Mean? A Semantic Identifiability Frontier for Pairwise Preference Learning
entry.summary: Pairwise comparison data are a standard supervision signal in preference learning, but disagreement in such data can reflect stable latent heterogeneity, ephemeral stochasticity, or non-binary responses hidden by a forced-choice interface. We study which of these semantic distinctions are identifiable from the feedback channel itself. We introduce a nonparametric latent semantic model with three querywise quantities: aggregate directional preference $μ_q$, persistent disagreement $τ_q$, and non-binary mass $α_q$. Under the anonymous binary channel, we prove an exact semantic fiber theorem: $μ_q$ is point-identified, whereas $(τ_q, α_q)$ vary over an explicit feasible region compatible with the same binary law. Same-annotator repeats identify $τ_q$ through a covariance identity, abstention-enabled feedback identifies $α_q$ directly, and together they point-identify the full semantic triple. We also derive finite-sample estimators, nonasymptotic concentration bounds, and semantics-aware action-recovery guarantees, and validate the theory on theorem-matched synthetic data.

entry.title: Auction-based allocation of routes in capacity-constrained networks
entry.summary: We study the route-set allocation problem between end nodes in capacity-constrained flow networks with transfer costs. We introduce an origin--destination (OD) bidding language, in which a participant bids for bounded conic combinations of inlet--outlet--quantity licences and the mechanism performs the routing through a network-flow optimising winner-determination problem. We then study payment rules for the OD mechanism. Under a restricted model with openly and uniformly priced sources and bidders who are indifferent to the source of the gas, the Vickrey--Clarke--Groves (VCG) payment is core-stable; the key structural fact is that in this regime some optimal aggregate flows never use a physical pipe in both directions, so the winner-determination problem reduces to a single-commodity network flow whose value is submodular in the set of active bidders. If source access is allowed to depend on the individual consumer -- a realistic feature, e.g. when gas deals are embedded in bilateral political bargaining -- the reduction fails and VCG payments may lie strictly outside the core. For this general model we propose a dual (nodal) pricing rule derived from the shadow prices of the flow-conservation constraints, and prove it is always core-stable, at the cost of dominant-strategy incentive compatibility. Illustrative examples accompany each result.

entry.title: No-Regret Learning in Stackelberg Security Games with an Unknown, Bounded Set of Attacker Types
entry.summary: In a repeated Stackelberg security game, a defender commits in every round to a randomized allocation of its resources, and an attacker, drawn from a set of types, best-responds. Existing no-regret guarantees assume that the defender knows this set of types in advance. We drop this assumption: the set of types is unknown, and its size is at most $K_{\max}$, an upper bound that the defender is not told. We show that what can be learned then depends on what the defender observes. If it observes the type of each attacker, an algorithm that adds types to its list as they appear achieves regret $\tilde O(nK_{\max}\sqrt{T})$ over $T$ rounds with $n$ targets, the same $\sqrt T$ rate as with known types, at an extra factor of only $\sqrt{K_{\max}}$ and without ever using $K_{\max}$. If it observes only the attacked target and types come from an infinite universe, no algorithm has sublinear regret: in a fixed three-target game every algorithm suffers regret at least $T-2$, even against a single attacker type, because it cannot tell which type it faces. If, in addition, it is told every $B$ rounds which types have appeared so far, sublinear regret returns, at $\tilde O(nK_{\max}^{4/3}T^{2/3}+K_{\max} B)$. The first term is the rate of the partial-information learner we use, and we show that the additive cost of the delay cannot be avoided.

entry.title: Accord: Schelling-Point Arbitration as a Composable Solana Primitive
entry.summary: Accord is an arbitration oracle on Solana. Any Solana program can create an application specific court (i.e. subaccord) and file disputes. A random jury of a specialized, stake-weighted juror pool reviews encrypted evidence and votes under commit--reveal. Jurors that vote with the final ruling earn fees and slashed stake. Jurors that vote against it lose stake. Appeals grow the panel stepwise from 3 to 31 jurors, which raises both the cost of maintaining a captured verdict and, under certain conditions, the probability of a correct majority. Each pool defines its own collateral mint and its own fee mint, so the economics can fit the application. This paper elaborates the mechanism, the incentive model, the residual trust assumptions, and the differences to the established court on EVM, Kleros. We further discuss implementation details that are Solana specific.

entry.title: Optimal Online Stochastic Matching
entry.summary: We resolve the problem of unweighted online stochastic matching with a known arrival law by establishing its optimal competitive ratio. For Poisson arrivals, we achieve $1-e/e^e\approx0.8206$, matching the upper bound of Chierichetti, Giacchini, Panconesi, and Vattani [ICALP 2025]. For exactly $n$ i.i.d.~arrivals, we obtain the same guarantee up to an additive $O(n^{-1/2})$ loss. Our key technical contribution is an exact correspondence between Poisson matching and exponential scheduling, preserving both online performance and the expected offline optimum. To prove the latter, we show that the distribution of the maximum of a random supermodular set function is determined by its joint distributions along chains of nested sets, a result of independent interest. This reduces the analysis to chains, where classical Poisson--exponential duality applies. The offline equivalence extends to arbitrary nonnegative edge weights. We then design a posterior allocation policy for exponential scheduling and use the correspondence to transfer its optimal competitive guarantee to online matching. Additionally, we show that the optimal competitive ratio under an unknown arrival law is strictly lower than $1-e/e^e$, establishing a strict separation between the known and unknown arrival models.

entry.title: Exact Cut Complexity of Equal-Length Proportional Cake Cutting
entry.summary: We study proportional cake cutting under an equal-length constraint, where each of $n$ agents must receive a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ that is worth at least $1/n$ to that agent. Our main result determines the exact worst-case number of cuts needed to guarantee such an allocation, namely $2n-2$ for every $n$. This improves on the previously known quadratic upper bound. The proof combines the constrained necklace-splitting theorem with a recursive assignment argument based on Hall's theorem. The same bound extends to the stronger requirement of envy-freeness when $n$ is a prime power, and an $O(n^{1.525})$ upper bound holds for arbitrary $n$. We then ask whether such allocations can be computed. We first show that no deterministic protocol in the Robertson--Webb model terminates after finitely many queries on every instance and always returns an exact equal-length proportional allocation, even for two agents with identical valuations. For every $\varepsilon>0$, however, $O(n^2/\varepsilon)$ queries suffice to produce an allocation in which every agent receives a bundle of length exactly $1/n$ and value at least $1/n-\varepsilon$, again using at most $2n-2$ cuts. Finally, we augment the Robertson--Webb model with two-knife queries. We show that recursive balanced halving attains the optimal bound of $2n-2$ cuts when $n$ is a power of two. For arbitrary $n$, we give a procedure using $O(n\log n)$ cuts.
entry.arxiv:comment: A preliminary version of this paper appeared in the proceedings of the 51st International Symposium on Mathematical Foundations of Computer Science (MFCS 2026)

entry.title: Effective-Balance Design in Ethereum Proof-of-Stake
entry.summary: Proof-of-Stake (PoS) systems offer a scalable and energy-efficient alternative to Proof-of-Work (PoW). The economic security of PoS relies critically on incentivizing broad and meaningful participation through well-cali\-brated staking reward mechanisms. We study Ethe\-reum's effective-balance rules as a mechanism-design problem in which the protocol chooses a reward coefficient, an activation threshold, and a maximum effective balance, and validators respond in the induced propor\-tional-allocation game. For fixed participating validators and identity counts, we establish a unique Nash equilibrium in validator-level total stakes. When validators can split or merge their visible identities, each candidate identity structure must be evaluated after the market re-clears. Restructuring incentives therefore depend on post-reset payoff comparisons that account for all validators' stake responses. For an illustrative simulation, we construct address-level budget proxies from Beacon Chain deposits and withdrawals, Lido staking flows, Etherscan balances, and calibrated synthetic agents. With illustrative cost coefficients, lowering the reserve price from 32 ETH to 30 ETH increases active identities by 5.922\% and total effective stake by 0.098\%.

entry.title: PPAD-Completeness of Contiguous Envy-Free Cake Cutting with Additive Valuations
entry.summary: We prove that computing a complete contiguous $\varepsilon$-envy-free cake allocation is PPAD-complete for normalized rational piecewise-constant additive valuations. The hardness holds even when $\varepsilon$ is given in unary, and even when every density takes only two values, which are the same for all agents, and is piecewise constant with at most six breakpoints. As a consequence, computing an exact contiguous envy-free allocation is also PPAD-complete, and the hardness holds under the same restrictions on the densities. Our key ingredient is to assign prices to the pieces so that, in every approximately envy-free allocation, all prices are nearly equal, regardless of how the pieces are assigned to the agents. We further show that, for every fixed integer $c\ge1$, computing a contiguous EF$c$ allocation of indivisible goods on a path is PPAD-complete for additive valuations, and the hardness holds even for binary valuations in which each good is valued by exactly one agent and all agents value the same number of goods.
entry.arxiv:comment: We prove that computing a contiguous envy-free cake division is PPAD-complete for additive valuations, and that computing a contiguous EF$c$ allocation of goods on a path is PPAD-complete for every fixed $c \geq 1$, resolving open questions of Goldberg, Hollender and Suksompong (JAIR 2020) and Bilò et al.\ (ITCS 2019)

entry.title: The Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-Complete
entry.summary: Poset games form a fundamental class of combinatorial games that includes classical games such as Nim and Chomp. Determining the outcome of a poset game is known to be PSPACE-complete even for posets of height at most three. However, the exact computational complexity of Two-Level Poset Game, played on posets of height at most two, has remained an open problem for over a decade. We resolve this problem by proving that Two-Level Poset Game is PSPACE-complete via a polynomial-time reduction from Avoid True on positive CNF formulas.

entry.title: What You Earn from What You Learn: Characterization and Complexity of the Value of Information
entry.summary: We examine the value of information in extensive-form decision problems: the largest multiplicative gain that a decision maker can obtain from an information refinement, taken over all payoff environments. This measures the structural importance of information disentangled from any particular payoff specification, and generalizes the notion of value of recall recently introduced by Berker et al. (AAAI'25). We establish a unifying characterization of the value of information under any information refinement, uncovering an intriguing connection to the maximum fractional chromatic number over a certain family of conflict graphs. We then employ our characterization to elucidate the complexity of two central information refinements. First, for the value of perfect information in perfect-recall decision problems, we find that the relevant conflict graphs are cographs, so the fractional chromatic number collapses to the clique number. Even though the clique number is tractable for a given cograph, we show that the additional layer of optimization (over the family of graphs) makes computing the value of perfect information NP-complete. On the positive side, we prove fixed-parameter tractability in terms of the degree of imperfect information. Second, for the value of recall in imperfect-recall decision problems (with no absentmindedness), we first show that the value of recall can realize the fractional chromatic number of any graph. Interestingly, this implies that, unlike the value of perfect information, the value of recall can take fractional values. Building on this reduction, we then establish S2P-completeness. This addresses questions left open by Berker et al. (AAAI'25)---both on the characterization and the complexity of the value of recall---and shows that computing the value of recall is strictly harder than the value of perfect information.

entry.title: Truthful and Expected-Payment-Optimal Model Routing in Graph-Based Agentic Workflows
entry.summary: Assigning routine tasks to cheaper large language model (LLM) providers can reduce generation cost, but switching providers may require processing accumulated context again. Keeping dependent tasks with the same provider can instead reuse eligible context. Graph-based workflows therefore couple routing decisions across tasks. Independent providers may also privately know their real-time unit costs and strategically misreport them. We formulate this routing problem as a single-parameter procurement auction and propose STAR (Strategy-proof Topology-aware Agent Routing), which minimizes virtual-cost-weighted graph workloads. Its allocation rule and payments, computed by integrating workload over possible cost reports, make truthful reporting utility-maximizing regardless of other providers' reports and cover each truthful provider's execution cost. With independent cost distributions and non-decreasing virtual costs, STAR additionally minimizes the user's expected total payment to providers. Controlled synthetic experiments separate the execution-cost benefit of topology awareness from the payment benefit of virtual-cost optimization: the former grows with fan-out and transferred payload, while the latter increases gradually along the tested prior-shape heterogeneity path. A paired sensitivity study quantifies how payment savings vary with prior misspecification while strategy-proofness is preserved.

entry.title: Learning in Strategic Queuing with Geometric Recharge: From Bandits to Systems
entry.summary: We study packet routing in queuing systems where queues act as selfish, myopic agents that use no-regret learning algorithms to select servers with unknown service rates. To model the small buffers used in data centers, we assume that each server has a single-packet buffer. Even such a tiny buffer already captures the features of buffering: routers can exploit multiple servers while accepted packets remain in service, but packets can occupy servers for multiple rounds, complicating future service and learning. We first analyze a single queue routing packets to $m$ buffered servers with service rates $μ_1, \dots, μ_m$. This setting is equivalent to an instance of the recharging bandits problem with geometric recharge. We prove that any no-regret learner achieves a long-run average throughput of at least the Hamacher sum of the server rates, and that this bound is tight. Consequently, a single no-regret queue is stable if and only if its arrival rate is below the Hamacher sum of the server rates. Moreover, comparing against an optimal policy, we show that any no-regret learner is at least $0.77$-competitive, which is also tight. We then study multi-queue systems where $n$ queues with arrival rates $λ_1, \dots, λ_n$, each at most $λ_{\max}$, compete for service from $m$ buffered servers. We show that the smallest overprovisioning factor that guarantees the system to be stable under high-probability no-regret learning is $\frac{1}{1-λ_{\max}}$. Equivalently, in terms of the total arrival and service rates, the condition $\sum_{i=1}^n λ_i < (1-λ_{\max})\sum_{j=1}^m μ_j$ is sufficient, and sometimes necessary, for stability under no-regret learning. In particular, for $λ_{\max} = 1/2$, this improves the upper bound of Abel et al. (EC 2026) from $3$ to $2$, matching their lower bound and resolving their open question.

entry.title: Maximin share allocations for two types of items
entry.summary: We study the fair allocation of indivisible items among $n$ agents with additive valuations (or costs) using the fairness notion of maximin share (MMS). Since MMS allocations do not always exist when $n > 2$, one direction in the literature has been to identify special classes of instances in which exact MMS allocations can be guaranteed. We show that, when items can be divided into two types of chores, MMS allocations always exist and can be computed in polynomial time using a novel geometric approach inspired by prior work in job scheduling. We further discuss how our technique extends to instances with two types of goods, as well as mixed instances consisting of one type of objective good and one type of objective chore.

entry.title: IR-PRM+ with Previous-Utility Prediction: Constant Regret and Best-Iterate Convergence
entry.summary: Regret matching (and its variants) and counterfactual regret minimization are central algorithms in practice for normal-form and extensive-form game solving. Yet these have historically lacked the stronger theoretical convergence guarantees available to optimistic and extra-gradient methods. Recent work introduced IREG-PRM+, a regret matching variant which does have strong theoretical convergence guarantees. However, it relies on a simultaneous, extra-gradient update. IREG-PRM+ is an instance of the more general IR-PRM framework, where empirically optimistic and alternating updates often have better performance. However, the prior extra-gradient analysis does not extend to these cases. We introduce a new approach that covers both settings. For simultaneous and alternating IR-PRM+ in finite two-player zero-sum matrix games, previous-utility prediction recovers the constant-regret and convergence-rate guarantees previously obtained with extra-gradient prediction: external regret bounded independently of T, an O(T^{-1}) average duality gap, and an O(T^{-1/2}) best-current-iterate gap. Moreover, the current duality gap vanishes and the current profile converges to the Nash equilibrium set. The key step bounds the component of consecutive strategy movement not controlled by the existing IR-PRM+ regret inequality using the relative growth of the nondecreasing regret-vector norm rho_t. Coupling this bound across the two players yields recurrences whose effective coefficient scales as 1/(rho_t^X rho_t^Y), preventing unbounded norm growth. We extend the analysis to finitely many simplex learners under a weighted Minty condition and, through the corresponding CFR variant IR-PCFR+, recover analogous guarantees for finite two-player zero-sum perfect-recall extensive-form games under the same full-reach condition as prior work.

entry.title: The Geography of (Concurrent) Block Proposing
entry.summary: The resilience and censorship resistance of a blockchain depend on where the validators and proposers of that blockchain physically operate. We study the economic incentives behind this location choice, both with a single proposer and with multiple concurrent proposers. Formally, we study a game where proposers first choose locations and then compete in a first-price auction for an opportunity whose common value is driven by information from geographically dispersed sources. A single proposer minimizes variance-weighted delay, locating at a weighted median of the sources and co-locating with any dominant one. By contrast, with two proposers, information both observe equally early earns no rent, and each proposer's expected profit is proportional to the standard deviation of the information it receives before its rival. We show that the location game admits the jointly unobserved variance as an ordinal potential, so global solutions of a weighted two-median problem are equilibria. With two sources, one proposer locates at each, however weak one is. With more proposers and at least as many sources, equilibrium locations are distinct under regular bidding. Multiple concurrent proposers thus do more than limit any single proposer's control over inclusion: by rewarding exclusive rather than shared information, they create an economic force toward geographic decentralization.

entry.title: CLS Hardness of 2D Min-Max Optimization with Product Constraints
entry.summary: We study the complexity of computing approximate first-order Nash equilibria in min-max optimization problems with one dimensional min and max players and product constraints. For black-box access to the objective, we prove that any algorithm requires $Ω(1/\sqrtε)$ queries to find an $ε$-first-order Nash point. In the white-box setting, we establish CLS-hardness by reducing from End-of-Potential-Line. These results show that even the simplest min-max setting with one dimensional min and max players is at least as hard as CLS and therefore does not admit polynomial-time algorithms unless $\mathsf{CLS}\subseteq \mathsf{P}$.

entry.title: Falsification-proof non-market allocation mechanisms
entry.summary: Relying on manipulable characteristics to target the allocation of resources is fraught with difficulties. Naively optimal rules lead to falsification and allocative inefficiency. Optimizing the rule for allocative efficiency while accounting for falsification typically induces falsification, at a heavy cost to the agents. Moreover, falsification generates negative externalities. We characterize optimal falsification-proof rules under a broad range of falsification technologies. We also provide an honesty condition under which they solve the unconstrained problem of a planner who maximizes a weighted sum of allocative surplus and agents' welfare.

entry.title: Linear Last-Iterate Convergence Rates for Optimistic Learning in Harmonic Games
entry.summary: We prove that the last iterate of Optimistic Follow-The-Regularized-Leader (OFTRL) converges at a linear rate to a Nash equilibrium in multiplayer harmonic games. Our result holds under a mild game-regularity condition and for a large family of regularizers, including entropy, Tsallis, and log-barrier. Our analysis is based on a dual perspective of OFTRL: we prove that the interaction between optimism and the global structure of harmonic games leads to the dissipation of an energy function along the dual iterates, for which we establish tight quantitative bounds. Our result also holds for the Extragradient FTRL variant.

entry.title: Strategic Multi-Agent Resource Allocation via Statistical Contracts
entry.summary: We study a class of strategic hypothesis testing problems in which a principal aims to allocate resources among competing agents who possess data or data-generating mechanisms that may be relevant to the principal's goals. Each agent can pay a participation cost to opt into a statistical contract, in which case they generate data from a private distribution and receive an allocation based on a predetermined (and publicly known) mechanism. Each agent is either "null" or "non-null" and the principal's goal is to design the contract to limit the allocation to the former while maximizing transactions with the latter. Using e-values, we define a "continuous-closure," a set of allocations which prevents null agents from profiting in expectation and provides post-hoc risk control for general loss functions under arbitrary dependence. When the loss is the fraction of resources allocated to null agents, the region admits polynomial-time linear optimization. We also give explicit, interpretable closed-form approximations, and we analyze participation from a non-null agent's perspective, giving conditions under which entry into the contract is profitable. Finally, we extend the framework to support online arrival of the agents, in which case the principal has to make irrevocable on-the-fly decisions, and provide a method which gives time-uniform error-control in this setting.

entry.title: When Does Opponent Modeling Pay Off? Spatial Inference Stabilises Reinforcement Learning under Partial Observability
entry.summary: Deep reinforcement learning agents in partially observable competitive games must act on beliefs about an unseen opponent's intent. We study a spatial opponent model: a transformer trained with hindsight-relabelled opponent goals that outputs a subgoal heatmap from the opponent's observed trajectory, fused early into a dueling double DQN. In symmetric constant-sum foraging games with partial observability, the module stabilises training. Plain TD(0) DQN suffers degenerate seeds in three of four one-step configurations, whereas the opponent-model agent never collapses and, wherever training succeeds, recovers the majority of the symmetric game value. Transfers zero-shot to a foraging opponent unseen by the learner, with a positive goal advantage over the baseline, and loses this edge exactly where an information argument predicts: against a full-information tracking adversary whose intent is the learner itself, and on resource-dense maps where both agents saturate. A blindfold ablation, zeroing the heatmap at deployment, decomposes the advantage into two mechanisms: training-time stabilisation, which dominates where the credit assignment is hard and survives blinding on the dense map, and deployment-time inference, whose reliance shrinks as fog thins on the sparse map. We conclude that opponent-goal inference is a stability-and-transfer mechanism whose value is governed by measurable boundary conditions: visibility (fog thickness), opponent intent, and resource density.

entry.title: Fresh at Decision, Stale at Action: Routing New Information to LLM Decisions Already Made
entry.summary: Freshness shapes an LLM decision at the moment it is made; the action it commits to is latent, carried out later, in a changing world. We therefore introduce a timestamp theory of decision validity and a decision ledger that realises it. Six timestamps define a decision; a freshness ceiling bounds what up-to-date evidence guarantees at action time, placing the remaining risk in information published afterwards. Accuracy then factorises into two capabilities: routing, which delivers that information to affected decisions before their revision deadlines, and temporal judgment, which reads it for the time of action. The ledger is persistent state holding each decision's times, evidence and background knowledge, indexed by watch conditions written at decision time. Controlled decision streams with exact labels confirm four predictions across five LLMs, from 8B to frontier scale: freshness alone yields exactly the accuracy the ceiling predicts; models act on decisive news once it arrives, so accuracy follows routing; the ledger's index sets what routing reaches, and watch conditions reach indirect dependencies at low exposure; and the remaining errors concern when a change takes effect. Freshness makes a decision right when it is made; routing and temporal judgment keep it right when it is carried out.

entry.title: Truthful Two-Facility Location with Candidate Locations in Metric Spaces
entry.summary: We study a truthful facility location problem in which agents have private positions in a metric space and known approval preferences over two distinct facilities. Each agent incurs a cost equal to her total distance from the facilities she approves. The goal is to locate the facilities at a given set of candidate locations so as to approximately minimize either the social cost or the max cost, while incentivizing the agents to report their positions truthfully. This problem was previously studied for line metrics and deterministic mechanisms. We first settle the approximation ratio of deterministic mechanisms for the social cost on the line by establishing a lower bound of $7$, matching the upper bound from previous work, and show that randomization leads to a strict improvement. For the max cost, we show that the previously known optimal deterministic guarantee of $3$ remains tight even for universally strategyproof mechanisms. We then turn to general metric spaces. For deterministic strategyproof mechanisms, we obtain tight approximation ratios of $2n-1$ for the social cost and $5$ for the max cost. We also show that randomization yields substantial improvements for both objectives: for the social cost, we obtain a tight characterization, while for the max cost we establish nearly matching upper and lower

entry.title: Exact power indices for plurality-voting ensembles
entry.summary: Plurality-voting ensembles aggregate the predictions of multiple base classifiers and output the most voted class, with ties typically broken at random. Despite the simple aggregation rule, attributing the impact of each base classifier to the ensemble's predictions is far from straightforward. That is, a single base classifier's impact depends on how it interacts with the votes of all other classifiers in the ensemble, for example, in resolving ties, and not only on its own predictions. We address the attribution problem using established tools from cooperative game theory, studying the Banzhaf and Shapley power indices for new games modeling plurality voting and random tie-breaking, for binary and multiclass classification settings. Computing power indices is, in general, intractable. Surprisingly, our methods, collectively named ENPOWER, enable the exact computation of Banzhaf and Shapley values in linear time for the binary classification setting and in low-degree polynomial time for the multiclass setting. The algorithms in ENPOWER rely on new combinatorial formulations of the Banzhaf and Shapley indices, yielding closed-form solutions for the binary case and ordinary generating function representations for the multiclass case. We validate empirically the methods in ENPOWER demonstrating their high applicability, providing attribution values not captured by existing methods. We apply the attribution of ENPOWER to: ensemble pruning and prompt-based ensembling of vision-language models.

entry.title: A Matroid Generalization of Weighted Popular Matching: Characterization and Algorithm
entry.summary: We study a problem that unifies two major generalizations of popular matchings in the one-sided preference model. In a bipartite graph in which each vertex, or applicant, on one side has preferences over the adjacent vertices, a matching is called popular if it does not lose a head-to-head election against any other matching. Since the seminal work of Abraham, Irving, Kavitha, and Mehlhorn, who gave the first polynomial-time algorithm for finding a popular matching, numerous generalizations of the popular matching problem have been investigated. Two prominent directions are weighted popular matchings, in which each applicant is assigned a voting weight, and popularity problems under matroid constraints. The former admits a polynomial-time algorithm due to Mestre, while the most general form of the latter is the popular common independent set problem, for which a polynomial-time algorithm is given by Kavitha, Makino, Schlotter, and Yokoi. In this paper, we introduce the weighted popular common independent set problem, which simultaneously generalizes weighted popular matchings and popular common independent sets. Our main result is the first polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. A key ingredient of the algorithm is a solution-independent characterization of weighted popular common independent sets, which we establish in this paper. As consequences of our algorithmic result, we obtain polynomial-time algorithms for several previously unresolved problems, including weighted popular matchings with matroid constraints and weighted popular branchings.

entry.title: Certifying Capacity and Gaps of the Rank-Dependent Gain-Sharing Framework for Ranking
entry.summary: The randomized primal-dual framework of Devanur, Jain, and Kleinberg (SODA 2013) splits each unit matching gain between endpoint dual variables according to the matched offline rank. The gain-sharing function affects the certificate but not Ranking's decisions. Keeping the splitting rule and expected edgewise feasibility criterion fixed, we define certifying capacity as the strongest uniform guarantee obtainable by functional optimization over a prescribed function class. Its shortfall from Ranking's actual competitiveness is the certifying gap. We study unweighted online bipartite matching under adversarial arrivals on graphs with online degree at most $d$ and on $d$-regular graphs. The optimized protocol is tight on both degree-one classes and in the unrestricted setting, but has a strictly positive gap on both degree-two classes, even over all measurable nonnegative complementary splits. In both degree-two settings, we determine Ranking's exact competitiveness and the exact certifying capacity over nondecreasing gain-sharing functions. For general $d$, we optimize over nondecreasing, right-continuous functions $f:[0,1]\to[0,1]$ with $f(1)=1$, using their probability-measure representation. Both the certifying capacity and actual competitiveness converge to $1-1/e$ in both instance families as $d\to\infty$. The resulting gap is at most $1/(2ed)+O(d^{-2})$ for online degree at most $d$; on $d$-regular graphs, it vanishes but is at least $(1/(2e)-o(1))/d$. These results distinguish function-class restrictions from limitations of the fixed protocol and motivate tighter randomized primal-dual frameworks.
